function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and pushes it to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR).  
After adding the files, you can commit and push them with the standard Git commands.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to your repo from here, but the instructions below will get you there.

---

## 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Create / update the following files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files and install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why node:18‑alpine?*  
> It’s a lightweight, production‑ready image that matches the Node.js version used in the repo (adjust if your `package.json` specifies a different major version).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml`) at the root:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *Image placeholder* – The image name uses the GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> Replace `${{ github.repository_owner }}` with your GitHub username or organization if you prefer a different registry.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` if it doesn’t exist, then add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Log in to GHCR
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Push Docker image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> *What this does*  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Installs Node.js 18 and your dependencies.  
> 3. Runs tests (remove the step if you don’t have tests).  
> 4. Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA.  
> 5. Logs into GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> 6. Pushes the image to GHCR.

> *Prerequisites*  
> - The repo must have a `package.json` and an `app.js` (or whatever entry point you use).  
> - The `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret is automatically available in Actions; no extra setup needed.

---

## 3. Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you already had a Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifests that you’re updating, just `git add` those updated files instead.

---

## 4. Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will run automatically on the `main` branch, building the Docker image and pushing it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the push, you should see:

1. A new **Actions** tab with a successful run.  
2. The Docker image in **Packages → Packages** (under your GitHub account) with the SHA tag.  
3. The `k8s.yaml` file in the repo (you can apply it with `kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml` if you have a cluster).

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., missing `app.js`, wrong Node version, etc.), let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
